newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa weighs private sector funding for water.
newsitem.headline: South Africa weighs private sector funding for water.

text.p: South Africa might set up a national water corporation in partnership with private investors to manage the funding of capital projects, Water Affairs and Forestry Minister Kader Asmal said on Monday.
Asmal told reporters in Cape Town that future water supply projects would be determined by human need rather than political expediency and ultimately would have to be paid for by consumers.
His department was not authorised, however, to borrow money for capital projects that would be paid back by user charges over a prolonged period.

One solution under consideration was to establish a "parastatal", a state-owned corporation similar to the Eskom energy utility, that would be authorised to raise money on domestic or international capital markets.
"We are thinking seriously of a parastatal that would be involved in capital development in association with the private sector," he said.
South Africa's state-owned corporations, all of them now destined for complete or partial privatisation, have issued bonds locally and abroad to fund major capital developments.

Asmal said his department expected to publish a draft Water Act in February incorporating a complete review of water law, including the assumption that water rights and property rights were rigidly linked.
He said the new law would be based on 14 to 17 principles, which would be put to President Nelson Mandela's cabinet for approval at its last meeting of the year in December.
"Is water allocation a vested property right? We are going to reconcile the property clause in our new constitution with the larger community interest...but I'm going to do it by agreement," he said.
Asmal said provision had to be made to reassess the allocation of water under apartheid, which largely or entirely excluded black communities.
He said the new law would establish water as a national resource which could not be owned and would underline the importance of water as a foundation for development.
The new law would create an obligation to conserve water and a local authority that failed to maintain leaky water pipes would find the work being done by the state at their expense.
Asmal said between 12 and 18 million South Africans did not have any access to clean water.
He released a report which revealed it could cost 9.5 billion rand to deliver clean water to within 200 metres of every person in the country.
